 I. INTRODUCTION
       This Reply Brief is submitted by Jason A. Howton, an individual intervenor, number 666,

appearing pro se. Intervenor Howton owns and resides on property in Bell County, Texas, near

Links F20 and F23, the links his case asks the Commission to avoid. Intervenor Howton does not

oppose the Project. He asks the Commission to certify a route that avoids Links F20 and F23, with

Routes 295 and 296 best meeting the statutory criteria and Routes 499 and 899 available as

alternatives that also avoid the Cedar Valley corridor.

       This brief is organized around the Preliminary Order Issues. Intervenor Howton addresses

Issues 1, 2-3, 4, 5-7, 8-10, and 11-13, and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department issue. He does

not address the remaining issues and takes no position on them.


II. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 1: ADEQUACY OF APPLICATION AND
NUMBER OF ROUTES
       Intervenor Howton does not challenge the adequacy of the Application or the number of

reasonably differentiated routes. The Administrative Law Judges found the Application and notice

sufficient in SOAH Order No. 7, and the deadline to contest route adequacy has passed. Intervenor

Howton notes only the limited significance of that determination for the questions that remain. A

finding that the route pool is adequate is a threshold conclusion that the Commission has before it

a sufficient number of reasonably differentiated routes to conduct a proper evaluation. It is not a

finding that any particular route within that pool best meets the statutory criteria, and it does not

validate Route 894 or Links F20 and F23. To the contrary, an adequate pool of differentiated routes

is precisely what makes Routes 295 and 296, and the other routes that avoid Links F20 and F23,

available to be selected. The question of which route best meets the criteria of PURA §

37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) is addressed under Preliminary Order Issues Nos. 8-

10 below.

 III. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES NOS. 2-3: NOTICE OF APPLICATION AND
NOTICE OF PUBLIC MEETING
           This proceeding added approximately 400 miles of new route links after the June 2025

public meetings, expanding the universe of affected landowners from approximately 2,800 to

approximately 4,200.1 That expansion included Links F04 and F20, the link at the center of

Intervenor Howton’s case.2 Landowners newly affected by Links F04 and F20 were not provided

a public meeting before Applicants filed this Application.

           The published-notice mechanism Applicants used did not meaningfully reach the affected

community here. Applicants’ notice affidavit lists publication in sixteen newspapers, including the

Temple Daily Telegram and the Belton Journal for Bell County.3 It does not include the Salado

Village Voice, the local newspaper serving the Salado community through which Route 894 runs,

and to which Intervenor Howton subscribes. The Temple Daily Telegram provides no delivery

service to Intervenor Howton’s address in Bell County. Intervenor Howton does not contend that

publication in these sixteen newspapers fails the technical requirements of 16 TAC § 22.52. He

raises the point for the same reason the notice-timing disparity matters: the manner in which notice

was published predictably under-reached the residents closest to the contested F-segment links,

compounding the participation gap described below.

created two classes of affected landowners with materially different opportunities to participate.

V. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES NOS. 5-7: NEED
           Intervenor Howton does not dispute that the Permian Basin needs reliable power. He

disputes whether the record establishes that the claimed need for this particular line, in both

directions it is said to serve, has been validated rather than assumed. On the record actually before

the Commission, it has not. The need case rests on a load forecast whose largest single component

has not materialized, and on a bidirectional reliability rationale that Applicants conceded, in

discovery, they have not studied in either direction.


    A. The Forecast’s Largest Load Component Has Not Materialized




                                  Reply Brief of Intervenor Jason A. Howton
                                                  Page 7 of 29
            The Permian Basin Reliability Plan that justifies this Project combined an oil-and-gas load

forecast with a forecast of additional non-oil-and-gas load totaling 11,695 MW. Applicants’ own

witness confirmed on cross-examination that approximately 59 percent of that additional non-oil-

and-gas load, the single largest component, was attributable to cryptocurrency mining.10

           The reliability of that forecast is itself in question on this record. Since the ERCOT’s March

2024 status report, they have adjusted their load-forecasting methodology that reduces officer-

letter-confirmed load to roughly 55.4 percent of forecasted megawatts with 54 to 55 percent of its

additional non-oil-and-gas load relying on officer-letter confirmation.11 When confronted with the

gap between forecast and confirmed load, Applicants’ witnesses did not establish that the forecast

load has materialized; they responded that the forecast is directed at 2030 and 2038 and declined

to answer whether the justification has shifted to other load categories.12 The concern this raises is

not that demand growth is impossible, but that the specific forecast used to size and justify a $1.68

billion, highest-voltage line rests substantially on load that, on ERCOT’s own contemporaneous

assessment, was largely unconfirmed.


       B. Applicants Have Not Validated the Bidirectional Reliability Need in Either
       Direction
           Applicants’ need case describes a line that must carry power in both directions: west-to-

east when west Texas generation is exported, and east-to-west when Permian Basin load draws on

central Texas generation. Intervenor Howton served a fourth set of requests for information

directed at whether either direction of that bidirectional function has been studied. The responses,

which Applicants stipulated may be treated as if filed under oath, establish that it has not.

VI. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES NOS. 8-10: ROUTING
        Routing is the heart of this proceeding and of Intervenor Howton’s case. Applicants

identify Route 894 as the route that best meets the criteria of PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC §

25.101(b)(3)(B). Intervenor Howton respectfully submits that the record does not support that

conclusion as against the alternatives that avoid Links F20 and F23, and that the Commission

should certify a route that avoids those links, with Routes 295 and 296 best meeting the statutory

criteria and Routes 499 and 899 available as alternatives that also avoid the Cedar Valley corridor.


     A. Routes 295 and 296 Better Satisfy the Controlling Routing Criteria
        Applicants present Route 894 as the best-meets route by emphasizing the two criteria on

which it is strongest, habitable structures and a per-mile cost figure, while giving less prominence

to the criteria on which it is among the weakest. A complete comparison, drawn entirely from

Applicants’ own filed route data, shows that Routes 295 and 296 better satisfy the controlling

routing criteria when the full statutory picture is considered.23

        Endangered species habitat. This is the clearest distinction in Applicants’ own data, and it

runs strongly in favor of Routes 295 and 296. Applicants’ filed route table reports that Routes 295

and 296 each cross 107 feet of habitat of federally listed endangered or threatened species, against

461 feet for Route 894, a reduction of approximately 77 percent. Environmental integrity is an

       B. The Stated Rationale for Link F20 Rests on Disfavored Future-Development

           There is a further and independent reason the Commission should decline to select a route

through Link F20. Applicants’ own Environmental Assessment states that Links F04 and F20 were

added as recommended alternatives avoiding a large-scale proposed development between FM

2843 and a potential future highway.32 The same table reflects that a related link, Link F03, was

future highway is the proposed Corridor J. Link F20 thus owes its existence to two

highway.

           The Commission has consistently held that speculative future development of this kind

cannot drive route selection. In Docket No. 51568, the presiding ALJs recognized, and the

Commission affirmed, that future development is not typically considered in route selection

because PURA and the Commission’s rules do not list future or potential development as factors

           The question is not whether the school is a factor. It is how much weight that single factor

should carry against the totality of the record, and whether the parties pressing it are applying a

consistent standard. On both points, the F34 concern does not displace Routes 295 and 296.

           1. The School Is One Factor in a Holistic Comparison, Not a Disqualifier
           As former Chairman Smitherman testified, the Commission weighs the totality of the

statutory factors and may not consider any factor or subset of factors in isolation.41 The parties

advancing the F34 argument ask the Commission to do precisely what that testimony forecloses:

treat one habitable structure, the school, as dispositive while setting aside the concentrated harms

Routes 295 and 296 avoid by not running through the Cedar Valley corridor on Links F20 and

F23. Those harms include impacts to existing homes, agricultural operations, churches, water

resources, and cultural resources, on a corridor that an EF-3 tornado tracked in April 2022. A
